title: Fill In a Sudoku Grid
statement:
You get a 9×9 sudoku board as a grid of single characters. A digit "1"–"9" is a given clue; "." is an empty cell.

Fill every empty cell in place so that each row, each column and each of the nine 3×3 boxes holds every digit 1–9 exactly once. The clues must stay as they are. Return nothing.

Every test board can be completed. If a board could be completed in more than one way, any valid completion is accepted.

examples.why: Forty empty cells. Some are forced at once (row 7 is missing only 2, 4 and 8), the rest need trial and error.

examples.in: board = a full grid except board[4][2] = "."
examples.why: Row 4 already has every digit except 4, so there is nothing to search.

constraints: The clues never repeat a digit in a row, column or box
hints: Try a digit in the first empty cell, move on, and undo the choice when you get stuck. What do you need to check before placing a digit?
Checking a row, column and box by scanning costs 27 reads per try. Keep three sets (or 9-bit masks) per row, column and box so the check is O(1).
Always fill the empty cell with the fewest legal digits next. A cell with one option is free, and a cell with zero options means you must back up right away.

explain.intuition:
Sudoku is a search: pick an empty cell, try a digit that does not clash, go on to the next cell, and if some later cell has no legal digit, undo the last choices and try the next digit. That is backtracking. The board itself is the state, so placing and removing a digit is the "do" and "undo".

Two things make it fast. First, keep which digits each row, column and box already uses, as bit masks, so legality is one AND instead of a scan. Second, choose the most constrained cell next. Real puzzles are full of cells with one option, and filling those first means the search rarely branches at all.
steps: Scan the board once. For every clue, set its bit in rowMask[r], colMask[c] and boxMask[b], and list the empty cells.
In the recursive step, look at every still-empty cell and pick the one with the fewest free digits (~(row | col | box) has the fewest bits).
If that cell has no free digit, return false. If no empty cell is left, return true.
Otherwise try each free digit: write it, set the three bits, recurse. If the recursion succeeds, stop. If not, clear the bits and the cell and try the next digit.
pitfalls: Forgetting to undo the bits or the cell after a failed branch. The next branch then sees digits that are not really there.
Computing the box index wrong. It is Math.floor(r / 3) * 3 + Math.floor(c / 3), not r / 3 + c / 3.
Building a new board for every recursive call. Change the one board in place and restore it on the way back.

complexity.time: Exponential in the worst case; fast on real puzzles
complexity.space: O(81) for the masks and the recursion

solutions.title: Plain backtracking, cell by cell
solutions.idea: Find the first empty cell, try 1–9, and check each try by scanning its row, column and box.
solutions.time: O(9^e) worst case, e = empty cells

solutions.title: Bit masks + most constrained cell first
solutions.idea: Track used digits per row, column and box as 9-bit masks. Always branch on the empty cell with the fewest options.
solutions.time: Exponential worst case, near-linear on typical puzzles
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def solveSudoku(self, board: List[List[str]]) -> None:
        rows, cols, boxes = [0] * 9, [0] * 9, [0] * 9
        empty = []
        for r in range(9):
            for c in range(9):
                if board[r][c] == ".":
                    empty.append((r, c))
                else:
                    bit = 1 << (int(board[r][c]) - 1)
                    rows[r] |= bit
                    cols[c] |= bit
                    boxes[r // 3 * 3 + c // 3] |= bit

        def solve(left):
            if left == 0:
                return True
            # pick the empty cell with the fewest free digits, move it to slot left - 1
            best, best_free, best_count = -1, 0, 10
            for i in range(left):
                r, c = empty[i]
                free = ~(rows[r] | cols[c] | boxes[r // 3 * 3 + c // 3]) & 0x1FF
                n = bin(free).count("1")
                if n < best_count:
                    best, best_free, best_count = i, free, n
                    if n <= 1:
                        break
            if best_count == 0:
                return False
            empty[best], empty[left - 1] = empty[left - 1], empty[best]
            r, c = empty[left - 1]
            b = r // 3 * 3 + c // 3
            free = best_free
            while free:
                bit = free & -free
                free ^= bit
                rows[r] |= bit
                cols[c] |= bit
                boxes[b] |= bit
                board[r][c] = str(bit.bit_length())
                if solve(left - 1):
                    return True
                rows[r] ^= bit
                cols[c] ^= bit
                boxes[b] ^= bit
            board[r][c] = "."
            return False

        solve(len(empty))

followups: How would you count the completions, to check that a puzzle has exactly one?
Before searching, fill every cell that has only one legal digit, and every digit that fits in only one place in a row. How much search is left on typical puzzles?
